title: Kafka internals
scopeHtml: Scope: partitions, replication, ISR, offsets, retention, compaction and sizing. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: The broker, partition and segment layout
notes.html:
A Kafka partition is a directory of segment files on a broker's disk; messages are appended sequentially. Each message gets an increasing offset within its partition. A segment (default log.segment.bytes = 1 GiB) is rolled when full or after log.roll.hours; old segments are deleted or compacted as whole files.

Why Kafka is fast: sequential disk writes, the OS page cache (the broker leans on it rather than its own heap cache), batching and compression, and zero-copy sendfile from page cache to the network socket. A modest broker can sustain hundreds of MB/s.

topic orders, partition 0
00000000000000000000.log   offsets 0..99,999
00000000000000100000.log   offsets 100,000..  (active segment)
each segment also has .index (offset->position) and .timeindex

Worked example. A topic gets 50 MB/s in. At 1 GiB segments, a new segment rolls about every 20 s. Reading a recent offset is served from RAM; reading data from 3 days ago hits disk and can evict hot pages for others (a known cause of latency spikes when a consumer replays history).

Industry examples. LinkedIn originally designed this layout; Kafka powers Uber, Netflix and most data platforms with the same storage design.

Everyday analogy. A notebook where each page is numbered; you only ever write at the end and bookmark where you stopped reading.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Kafka is fast because it is "in memory". It is disk-based, sequential, and relies on page cache.
  • Using a huge number of tiny partitions; each costs file handles and metadata.

notes.title: Replication, leader and ISR
notes.html:
Each partition has one leader and N-1 follower replicas on other brokers. Producers and consumers talk to the leader; followers copy from it. The ISR (in-sync replicas) is the set of replicas caught up with the leader (within replica.lag.time.max.ms, default 30 s in recent versions; confirm for your version).

Key settings:

  • replication.factor=3
  • min.insync.replicas=2
  • Producer acks=all (or -1): the leader waits for all ISR members to have the write.

With RF=3, min.insync=2, acks=all: you survive 1 broker loss without data loss and without losing availability for writes. If the ISR shrinks to 1, writes are rejected (NotEnoughReplicas) rather than accepting data that is not safely stored. unclean.leader.election.enable=false (the default) prevents an out-of-sync replica from becoming leader, trading availability for no data loss.

acks Meaning Risk
0 Fire and forget Lost on any failure
1 Leader wrote it Lost if leader dies before followers copy
all All ISR wrote it Safe up to min.insync loss

Gravity. The replication factor cannot easily be changed without reassigning partitions; choose 3 up front for important topics (a costly-to-reverse, but doable, operation). Cross-AZ placement (broker.rack) lets you survive a zone loss.

Industry examples. Banks and payment companies run RF=3, min.insync=2, acks=all. Metrics: UnderReplicatedPartitions greater than 0 is the classic alarm.

Everyday analogy. Writing the meeting minutes and getting two colleagues to confirm their copies before declaring "saved".

Common interview traps.

  • acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1 gives no extra safety once the ISR drops to the leader alone.
  • Enabling unclean election for availability and silently losing committed messages.

notes.title: Offsets and commits
notes.html:
An offset is a consumer's bookmark per partition. Committed offsets are stored in the internal topic __consumer_offsets, per (group, topic, partition). The committed value is the next offset to read.

  • Auto-commit (enable.auto.commit=true, every 5 s by default): easy, but it can commit before processing finishes (loss on crash) or after (duplicates).
  • Manual commit after processing: at-least-once. Commit before processing: at-most-once.
  • auto.offset.reset=earliest|latest decides where a brand-new group starts.
  • Lag = latest offset minus committed offset; the key health metric.
while (true) {
  var records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
  for (var r : records) handle(r);       // must be idempotent
  consumer.commitSync();                 // commit after processing
}

Worked example. Handler takes 40 ms per record, poll returns 500 records: 20 s of work. If max.poll.interval.ms is 300 s you are fine; if it is 10 s the consumer is kicked from the group, a rebalance happens and the batch is processed again by someone else. Lower max.poll.records or speed up the handler.

Industry examples. Every Kafka consumer app (Spring Kafka, Kafka Streams). Tools: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group billing shows lag per partition.

Everyday analogy. A bookmark: move it only after you actually finished the page.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a commit means "processed" rather than "I promise I will start here".
  • Long processing causing rebalance storms from max.poll.interval.ms.

notes.title: Retention and log compaction
notes.html:
Kafka deletes by time or size, or keeps only the latest value per key (compaction).

  • Delete policy: retention.ms (default 7 days), retention.bytes. Deletion works on whole segments, so data may live a little longer than the limit.
  • Compact policy (cleanup.policy=compact): for each key, keep at least the latest record; older ones are removed in the background. A tombstone (key with null value) marks a deletion and is itself removed after delete.retention.ms. The newest active segment is not compacted.
  • Both: cleanup.policy=compact,delete.
Before compaction:  k1=a, k2=b, k1=c, k3=d, k2=null
After compaction:   k1=c, k3=d          (k2 tombstoned then removed)

Use cases. Compaction suits changelogs and state: a "user profile" topic, KTable backing topics in Kafka Streams, __consumer_offsets itself, CDC from a database (rebuild current state from the topic). Delete retention suits event streams (clicks, logs).

Worked example. Config topic with 10M updates for 200k keys: after compaction roughly 200k records remain, so a new consumer bootstraps in seconds rather than replaying 10M.

Industry examples. Debezium CDC topics, Kafka Streams state stores, Schema Registry's _schemas topic.

Everyday analogy. A contacts list: you keep only the latest phone number per person, not every number they ever had.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting compaction to be immediate or to remove all old values instantly.
  • Keys must not be null in compacted topics.
  • Treating tombstones as instant deletes (consumers must still see them for the retention window).

notes.title: Sizing a Kafka cluster
notes.html:
Size by throughput, retention and consumer parallelism. Work through the numbers.

Worked example. 20,000 msgs/s at 1 KB = 20 MB/s ingest. Retention 7 days, RF=3.

  • Daily data: 20 MB/s x 86,400 = about 1.73 TB. Seven days = about 12.1 TB.
  • With RF=3: about 36.3 TB raw. Add 30% headroom: about 47 TB. On brokers with 8 TB usable each, about 6 brokers.
  • Network: ingest 20 MB/s, replication adds 2 x 20 = 40 MB/s out of leaders to followers, consumers (say 3 groups) read 60 MB/s. About 120 MB/s per cluster, split over 6 brokers: easy for 10 GbE.
  • Partitions: target throughput per partition is about 5 to 10 MB/s write for one partition (varies, benchmark). For 20 MB/s, 6 partitions suffice for ingest; but if each consumer handles 2,000 msgs/s, you need 10 consumers, so choose 12 to 24 partitions for headroom and parallelism. A rough guide is a few thousand partitions per broker as a ceiling (newer KRaft versions handle many more; confirm for your version).

Config levers: compression (lz4 or zstd, 2 to 4x smaller for JSON), linger.ms=5-20 with batch.size=64KB for throughput.

Gravity. Partition count is easy to increase and effectively impossible to decrease; start moderately (for example 12), grow later. Over-partitioning increases rebalance time and recovery.

Industry examples. LinkedIn reported trillions of messages/day; Uber and Netflix run multi-cluster setups with MirrorMaker or Replicator for cross-region.

Everyday analogy. Planning warehouse shelves: how fast boxes arrive, how long you keep them, and how many copies you store.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the RF multiplier on disk and network.
  • Choosing partitions from broker count rather than consumer parallelism and per-partition throughput.
  • Ignoring that ZooKeeper has been replaced by KRaft in modern Kafka (ZooKeeper removed in 4.0).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Partition = ordered segmented log on disk; speed comes from sequential I/O, page cache, batching, zero-copy.
  • RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, no unclean election for safe durability.
  • Offsets are consumer bookmarks in __consumer_offsets; commit after processing gives at-least-once.
  • Retention deletes whole segments by time/size; compaction keeps the latest value per key, with tombstones for deletes.
  • Size from MB/s x retention x RF; choose partitions from consumer parallelism; partitions can grow, not shrink.
